extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, journalists, communicators, and policymakers studying public opinion, propaganda, and persuasion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria about how public opinion is formed, communicated, and manipulated — including sampling biases, stereotyping, dramatization, visualization, and appeals to emotion and self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and selection awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: We are so little trained in the selection of our samples... In dealing with any large mass of facts, the presumption is against our having picked true samples, if we are acting on a casual impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims by checking how representative the evidence is. Beware of drawing general conclusions from easily available, convenient, or small samples (e.g., 'the first six people we meet'). Anti-pattern: treating anecdotal, convenience, or self-selected examples as if they were random or representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding post hoc causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: the commonest form of reasoning is the intuitive, post hoc ergo propter hoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer cause simply from sequence or co-occurrence. When analyzing public events or policy effects, demand stronger evidence of causal mechanisms rather than relying on intuitive sequence-based explanations. Example anti-pattern: assuming X caused Y just because Y followed X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional association can fabricate causal links
rubrics_metrics.description: When two ideas that come together arouse the same feeling... anything can be related to anything else, provided it feels like it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that emotional contiguity (shared feeling) can cause people to link unrelated phenomena as cause/effect. In evaluation, separate emotional resonance from evidentiary connection. Example: linking social ills to a single hated object because both provoke fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use qualifiers; avoid absolutism
rubrics_metrics.description: We prefer most to more, least to less, we dislike the words rather, perhaps, if, or, but, toward, not quite, almost, temporarily, partly. Yet nearly every opinion about public affairs needs to be deflated by some word of this sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor nuanced, qualified assertions in public claims and analysis. Anti-pattern: grand, absolute claims ('this will end war forever') that ignore complexity and invite backlash or disillusionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization and dramatization of abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: we tend to personalize quantities, and to dramatize relations... Social Movements, Economic Forces, National Interests, Public Opinion are treated as persons
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convey abstract or complex issues, transform them into humanized narratives or personifications to aid comprehension and empathy. But be aware this can oversimplify and distort structural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and concrete metaphors for comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures have always been the surest way of conveying an idea, and next in order, words that call up pictures in memory... human qualities... tend to be visualized in physical metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid imagery and concrete metaphors (e.g., a nation as 'John Bull', migration as a 'river') to make ideas memorable and to enable identification. Caveat: such metaphors can caricature nuance and mislead if taken literally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear handles for audience identification
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular representation the handles for identification are almost always marked. You know who the hero is at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make protagonists/antagonists or points of identification explicit so broad audiences can quickly latch on. Anti-pattern: ambiguous or abstruse framing that fails to provide an entry point for general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide audience with something to do (engagement via action)
rubrics_metrics.description: the audience must have something to do, and the contemplation of the true, the good and the beautiful is not something to do... the audience must be exercised by the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages and representations that invite mental engagement (taking sides, anticipating outcomes) rather than passive contemplation. Use stakes, choices, or suspense to mobilize interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of suspense, conflict, and primal motifs to sustain interest
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two forms of exercise which far transcend all others... sexual passion and fighting... a fight about sex outranks every other theme in the breadth of its appeal... Politics is interesting when there is a fight, or as we say, an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict, suspense, and elemental motifs (sex, struggle) reliably capture and hold attention. Ethical caution: manufacturing or exaggerating conflict to engage audiences can distort reality and polarize unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance realism with romantic/desired resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: popular taste is to have the drama originate in a setting realistic enough to make identification plausible and to have it terminate in a setting romantic enough to be desirable... a true beginning and the happy ending are landmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting persuasive narratives, start from plausible, familiar premises and offer an appealing, hopeful outcome—too much realism can repel, too much fantasy can fail to engage. Anti-patterns: pure fantasy without footholds; relentless realism that offers no resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work within or cautiously alter stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: The stereotypes can be altered, but not in time to guarantee success when the film is released six months from now... men who make moving pictures... must adhere to the stereotypes that they find, or pay the price of frustrating expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize prevailing stereotypes and cultural expectations; aligning with them improves uptake, while attempting to change them is a long-term, risky endeavor. Innovators who alter stereotypes may succeed but face resistance and commercial constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible beginning then utopian promise as a propaganda formula
rubrics_metrics.description: the skilful propagandist knows that while you must start with a plausible analysis, you must not keep on analyzing... then stokes up energy for a long voyage by brandishing a passport to heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert that persuasive campaigns often combine credible-seeming facts with grand promises of a transformed future. In evaluation, separate the plausible diagnosis from speculative, emotionally enticing promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect variation of interpretation across diverse audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: the identical story is not the same story to all who hear it... the more mixed the audience, the greater will be the variation in the response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniform reception; messages are reinterpreted through varied experiences, vocabularies, and 'common words' of different groups. Tailor communication or anticipate divergent readings across demographics and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify which 'self' or identity an appeal targets
rubrics_metrics.description: "self-interest" determines opinion... the statement is not illuminating, until we know which self out of many selects and directs the interest so conceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that individuals possess multiple selves (e.g., parent, patriot, worker) and that appeals should be crafted to engage the particular self relevant to the issue. Anti-pattern: generic appeals that ignore role-specific motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and role shape character and response
rubrics_metrics.description: The selves... take their form from a man's conception of the situation in which he finds himself... The character he gives it varies... according to... sex and age, race and religion and social position... his moods and tenses, or his place on the board in any of the games of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how situational frames (status, role, social expectations) modulate opinions and behaviors. Effective messaging accounts for context-driven character shifts; research should measure responses across roles and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational triggers can release repressed impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: repression is not irretrievable. For just as psychoanalysis can bring to the surface a buried impulse, so can social situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that extraordinary contexts (war, crisis, public spectacles) can activate latent attitudes or impulses not apparent in normal times. Predictive models should include potential activation of buried sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories and rumors are fluid; messages mutate in transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: the original story, true or invented, grows wings and horns, hoofs and beaks, as the artist in each gossip works upon it... rumor... the original story... grows as it is passed on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect factual narratives to be edited, embellished, and reinterpreted as they circulate. Communication strategies should account for distortion over chains of transmission and incorporate corrective or anchoring mechanisms.
